abstract: This paper by Fregin and colleagues at Maastricht University synthesizes micro-level evidence from firm and worker studies on the adoption and impact of generative AI in daily business operations. The synthesis finds that most firms using generative AI report modest productivity gains in the range of 5-15%, with effects concentrated in text-heavy and analytical tasks (e.g., drafting, summarization, data analysis, customer communication) rather than in transformative business model changes. The review draws on multiple empirical studies spanning field experiments, firm surveys, and worker-level productivity measurements to build a composite picture of how generative AI is actually being used in practice versus theoretical predictions. The central finding — that GenAI's real-world productivity impact is modest, task-specific, and incremental — provides an important counterweight to both hype-driven narratives of AI transformation and pessimistic predictions of mass displacement. The evidence suggests that GenAI is functioning primarily as a productivity tool within existing workflows rather than as a catalyst for fundamental reorganization of work.
keyFindings: Most firms using generative AI report productivity gains of 5-15%, modest relative to more optimistic projections but consistent across multiple studies and methodologies.

Productivity effects are concentrated in text-heavy and analytical tasks (drafting, summarization, data analysis, customer communication) rather than in strategic decision-making or business model innovation.

GenAI is functioning primarily as an incremental productivity tool within existing workflows rather than a catalyst for fundamental business transformation, at least in the current early-adoption period.
The synthesis reveals a gap between the theoretical potential of GenAI (broad task automation) and its practical deployment (narrow task augmentation within established processes).

Worker-level evidence is broadly consistent with firm-level evidence: individual productivity gains are real but modest, with the largest effects among less-experienced workers performing routine analytical tasks.
methodology: Systematic synthesis of micro-level empirical studies on generative AI adoption and productivity impact, including randomized field experiments, firm-level surveys, and worker-level productivity measurements. The review covers studies from multiple countries and industries, focusing on evidence published since the release of ChatGPT (November 2022). Published by Maastricht University, 2026.
qualifiers: The synthesis covers early-adoption-period evidence, and productivity effects may increase as firms learn to integrate GenAI more deeply. Publication bias may skew the included studies toward those finding measurable effects. Most micro-level studies cover a limited set of tasks and occupations, and extrapolation to the broader economy requires caution. The 5-15% range spans considerable variation across studies, tasks, and worker types. Methodological heterogeneity across synthesized studies limits the precision of aggregate conclusions.
